stem:
A 41-year-old woman, a choir singer, returns 2 weeks after a total thyroidectomy.
Chief complaint: "I can't reach my high notes anymore."
Findings: her voice is weak and monotone; she is not hoarse, and both vocal folds move on laryngoscopy.
Injury to which nerve best explains this?
ex: The external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery and is at risk when that artery is tied. It supplies the cricothyroid, the tensor of the vocal folds, so its loss gives a weak, monotone voice that can't reach high pitches. The recurrent laryngeal nerve, beside the inferior thyroid artery, causes hoarseness when injured.
why: This nerve runs near the inferior thyroid artery; its injury paralyzes most intrinsic laryngeal muscles and causes hoarseness and a fold that doesn't move.
It runs with the superior thyroid artery and supplies the cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal folds to raise pitch.
It is sensory to the larynx above the vocal folds; its loss impairs the cough reflex, not pitch.
It supplies the strap muscles; weak straps don't take away the voice's range.
It moves the tongue; it has no role in tensing the vocal folds.

likely.t: Nerves at risk in thyroid surgery and the carotid sheath and its neighbors

stem:
A 64-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history has a mass at the apex of his right lung on chest film.
Findings: his right upper eyelid droops slightly and the right side of his face is dry and flushed.
Each of the following is expected on the right side EXCEPT:
choices: Loss of sweating on the face
ex: An apical (Pancoast) tumor can compress the cervical sympathetic chain and cause Horner syndrome on the same side: partial ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and flushing. The pupil is small, never dilated; a dilated pupil with full ptosis points to CN III instead.
why: The pupil is small (miosis), because the sympathetic dilator pupillae is paralyzed and the parasympathetic sphincter is unopposed.
Expected: the superior tarsal muscle, a sympathetic smooth muscle that helps hold the lid up, is paralyzed.
Expected: the sweat glands of the face lose their sympathetic supply (anhidrosis).
Expected: the skin's vessels lose sympathetic tone and dilate.

likely.t: Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and flushing from a cervical sympathetic lesion

stem: During a neck dissection, which structure is found just posterior to the carotid sheath, embedded in the prevertebral fascia, rather than inside the sheath?
ex: The carotid sheath holds the common and internal carotid arteries medially, the IJV laterally and the vagus between and behind them, with the deep cervical nodes along the vein. The sympathetic trunk is outside the sheath, behind it, in the prevertebral fascia.
why: The vagus is inside the sheath, posterior and between the artery and the vein.
The IJV is the lateral content of the sheath.
It lies behind the sheath on the prevertebral fascia, which is why it is spared when the sheath is opened but involved by tumors pressing from behind.
The common carotid is the medial content of the sheath.
They run along the IJV, in and around the sheath, not in the prevertebral fascia.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The superior root of the ansa cervicalis carries C1 fibers that run with the hypoglossal nerve for part of their course.
2. The anterior belly of the digastric and the mylohyoid are both supplied by the nerve to the mylohyoid, a branch of V3.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: The ansa cervicalis has a superior root (C1, carried by XII) and an inferior root (C2–C3) and supplies the strap muscles. The anterior digastric and mylohyoid (arch 1) get the nerve to the mylohyoid from V3; the posterior digastric and stylohyoid (arch 2) get VII.
why: Statement 1 is true: C1 fibers hitch a ride on XII and leave it as the superior root; they are not hypoglossal fibers. Statement 2 is true: the nerve to the mylohyoid leaves the inferior alveolar nerve just before the mandibular foramen and supplies both arch 1 muscles.

Statement 1 is true, not false: C1 fibers hitch a ride on XII and leave it as the superior root; they are not hypoglossal fibers. Statement 2 is true, not false: the nerve to the mylohyoid leaves the inferior alveolar nerve just before the mandibular foramen and supplies both arch 1 muscles.
Statement 2 is true, not false: the nerve to the mylohyoid leaves the inferior alveolar nerve just before the mandibular foramen and supplies both arch 1 muscles.
Statement 1 is true, not false: C1 fibers hitch a ride on XII and leave it as the superior root; they are not hypoglossal fibers.

likely.t: Suprahyoid and infrahyoid nerves, landmarks, carotid sinus and fascial spaces

stem: True or false: The thoracic duct empties into the venous system where the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins meet.
ex: The thoracic duct starts at the cisterna chyli, climbs through the thorax and arches in the root of the neck to the left venous angle. It drains everything except the right upper quadrant, which the right lymphatic duct drains.
why: The left venous angle, the union of the left IJV and left subclavian vein, is where the thoracic duct ends.
The statement is correct: the duct ends at the left venous angle; the right lymphatic duct is the one on the right.

likely.t: Root of the neck: subclavian branches, phrenic nerve, thoracic duct and the superior thoracic aperture

stem: True or false: The phrenic nerve descends on the anterior surface of the middle scalene muscle.
ex: The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) forms at the lateral border of the anterior scalene and runs down its anterior surface, then between the subclavian artery and vein into the thorax. The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalenes.
why: The muscle is wrong: the phrenic nerve lies on the anterior scalene.
The phrenic nerve lies on the anterior scalene, not the middle scalene; the brachial plexus is what lies against the middle scalene.

stem:
Which are branches of the first part of the subclavian artery (medial to the anterior scalene)?
1. Vertebral artery
2. Internal thoracic artery
3. Costocervical trunk
4. Thyrocervical trunk
ex: First part: vertebral (enters the C6 transverse foramen), internal thoracic and thyrocervical trunk. Second part, behind the anterior scalene: costocervical trunk. Third part: the dorsal scapular, when it arises there.
why: It includes 3, which is false: the costocervical trunk comes from the second part, behind the anterior scalene. It leaves out 4, which is true: the thyrocervical trunk leaves the first part and gives the inferior thyroid, transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries.
It includes 3, which is false: the costocervical trunk comes from the second part, behind the anterior scalene.
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are true. Statement 3 is false: the costocervical trunk comes from the second part, behind the anterior scalene.
It leaves out 1, which is true: the vertebral artery is the first and largest branch of the first part.

stem: Which statement about the fascial spaces of the neck is true?
choices: The danger space lies between the alar and prevertebral fascia and reaches the diaphragm
The retropharyngeal space lies between the prevertebral fascia and the vertebral bodies
The pretracheal fascia wraps the SCM and trapezius
The carotid sheath contains the cervical sympathetic trunk
ex: Retropharyngeal space: buccopharyngeal fascia in front, alar fascia behind, from the skull base to the upper mediastinum. Danger space: alar fascia in front, prevertebral fascia behind, to the diaphragm. Both can carry infection from the teeth, tonsils and pharynx into the chest.
why: This is why an infection that enters the danger space can descend into the posterior mediastinum.
That describes the prevertebral space; the retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal and alar fascia.
The investing layer wraps the SCM and trapezius; the pretracheal layer wraps the thyroid, trachea and esophagus.
The sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath, in the prevertebral fascia.

stem:
A 35-year-old man had a lymph node removed from the posterior triangle of his neck 1 month ago.
Chief complaint: his shoulder aches and he can't lift his arm above his head well.
Findings: the shoulder droops on that side and shrugging against resistance is weak; turning the head is normal.
Which nerve was most likely injured?
ex: CN XI is the most vulnerable structure in the posterior triangle because it lies so superficially. Its injury paralyzes the trapezius: drooping shoulder, weak shrug and trouble raising the arm above the head.
why: It is a sensory nerve to the skin over the parotid and ear; it moves no muscle.
It lies deep on the anterior scalene and supplies the diaphragm, not the shoulder.
It crosses the posterior triangle just under the investing fascia, on the levator scapulae, and supplies the trapezius; the SCM branch usually leaves before this point, so head turning is spared.
Its injury causes winging of the scapula (serratus anterior), not a dropped shoulder with weak shrug.
It supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus; it doesn't cause a weak shrug.

likely.t: Posterior triangle: CN XI and the cervical plexus at the nerve point

stem: After a facelift, a patient has numbness of the skin over the angle of the mandible and the lower part of the ear. Which nerve carries sensation from this area?
ex: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) emerges at the nerve point on the posterior border of the SCM and supplies the skin over the parotid, the angle of the mandible and the lower auricle. The angle of the mandible is not supplied by the trigeminal nerve.
why: This cervical plexus branch supplies the skin over the parotid, the angle of the mandible and the lower ear; the angle is the one part of the face the trigeminal nerve doesn't cover.
It supplies the skin of the temple and the front of the ear, not the angle of the mandible.
It supplies the skin and mucosa of the cheek over the buccinator.
It supplies the chin and lower lip.
It supplies the skin of the front of the neck, below the mandible.

stem: Where are the cell bodies of the postganglionic sympathetic neurons that supply the dilator pupillae and the superior tarsal muscle?
ex: Sympathetic supply to the head: presynaptic neurons in the lateral horn of T1–T2, synapse in the superior cervical ganglion, postganglionic fibers along the internal and external carotid plexuses to the dilator pupillae, superior tarsal muscle, sweat glands and vessels.
why: Presynaptic fibers from T1–T2 ascend the trunk and synapse here; postganglionic fibers then ride the carotid arteries to the eye.
The ciliary ganglion holds parasympathetic (CN III) cell bodies for the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle; sympathetic fibers pass through it without synapsing.
That is where the presynaptic neurons sit; the postganglionic cell bodies are in a ganglion.
This is a parasympathetic ganglion of VII for the lacrimal and nasal glands.
This brainstem nucleus holds presynaptic parasympathetic neurons of CN III.

likely.t: Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and flushing from a cervical sympathetic lesion

stem: At what vertebral level is the cricoid cartilage, where the larynx becomes the trachea and the pharynx becomes the esophagus?
ex: Landmarks: hyoid C3, thyroid cartilage C4–C5, cricoid C6 (trachea and esophagus begin), tracheal bifurcation near T4–T5.
why: The cricoid cartilage, the start of the trachea and the start of the esophagus all sit at C6.
C3 is the level of the hyoid bone.
C4 is about the level of the upper thyroid cartilage, where the common carotid usually splits.
T1 is the back of the superior thoracic aperture.
T4 is about where the trachea divides into the main bronchi.

stem: True or false: The internal carotid artery gives off no branches in the neck.
ex: The ICA runs up to the carotid canal without branching in the neck; its first branch is the ophthalmic artery inside the skull. Any branching artery in the carotid triangle belongs to the external carotid.
why: No branches in the neck is the rule for the ICA: its first branch is the ophthalmic artery.
The statement is correct; it is the external carotid that branches in the neck.

stem: Each of the following passes through the superior thoracic aperture EXCEPT the:
ex: The superior thoracic aperture (T1, first ribs, manubrium) passes the trachea, esophagus, great arteries and brachiocephalic veins, vagus and phrenic nerves and the thoracic duct. The brachial plexus and subclavian vessels leave for the upper limb through the apex of the axilla.
why: The plexus passes over the first rib into the axilla, through the apex of the axilla, not into the thorax.
The esophagus passes from the neck into the superior mediastinum through the aperture.
The duct climbs out of the thorax through the aperture to reach the left venous angle.
It rises from the aortic arch through the aperture into the neck.
It enters the thorax through the aperture between the subclavian artery and vein.

stem:
A 70-year-old man faints while shaving with his head turned and pressure on the side of his neck at the level of the upper thyroid cartilage.
Vitals on arrival: pulse 48, BP 88/50.
Stimulation of which receptor, and which nerve, best explains the episode?
choices: Aortic arch chemoreceptors, through the phrenic nerve
Jugular baroreceptors, through the hypoglossal nerve
Carotid sinus baroreceptors, through the glossopharyngeal nerve
Carotid body chemoreceptors, through the vagus
ex: The carotid sinus, a dilation of the proximal internal carotid at the bifurcation, holds baroreceptors that report through the carotid sinus branch of IX. Outside pressure (a tight collar, shaving, massage) can set off reflex bradycardia and hypotension. The carotid body holds chemoreceptors.
why: The phrenic nerve is motor to the diaphragm and carries no baroreceptor input.
There are no named baroreceptors in the IJV, and XII is motor to the tongue.
Pressure on the sinus is read as high blood pressure; the reflex slows the heart and drops the pressure.
The carotid body senses blood oxygen and mainly drives breathing; pressure doesn't trigger it.

stem:
A 19-year-old man is struck on the side of the head with a baseball.
History: he was briefly knocked out, then talked normally for an hour.
Now: worsening headache, drowsiness, a dilated right pupil.
CT: a biconvex (lens-shaped) collection under the right temporal bone that does not cross the sutures.
The torn vessel entered the cranial cavity through which opening?
ex: A blow to the pterion tears the middle meningeal artery, which enters through the foramen spinosum. Arterial blood strips the dura off the skull, making a lens-shaped epidural hematoma, classically after a lucid interval.
why: The foramen ovale carries V3 and an emissary vein, not the artery torn in an epidural bleed.
The internal carotid artery passes here; its branches bleed into the subarachnoid space, not the epidural space.
The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters here and runs deep to the pterion; its tear gives an epidural hematoma.
This is the exit of the sigmoid sinus as the IJV and of IX, X and XI.
It is filled with cartilage in life and transmits no major artery.

likely.t: Foramina of the skull and what passes through each (rotundum, ovale, spinosum, jugular foramen)

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The superior and inferior petrosal sinuses empty into the cavernous sinus.
2. Blood in the superior sagittal sinus reaches the internal jugular vein by way of the confluence, transverse and sigmoid sinuses.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: The cavernous sinus receives the ophthalmic veins and drains backward through the petrosal sinuses. Most venous blood goes superior sagittal → confluence → transverse → sigmoid → IJV.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: the petrosal sinuses drain the cavernous sinus: the superior to the transverse/sigmoid sinus and the inferior to the IJV.
Statement 2 is true, not false: that is the main route of venous outflow from the brain, leaving the skull at the jugular foramen.

Statement 1 is false, not true: the petrosal sinuses drain the cavernous sinus: the superior to the transverse/sigmoid sinus and the inferior to the IJV. Statement 2 is true, not false: that is the main route of venous outflow from the brain, leaving the skull at the jugular foramen.

Statement 1 is false: the petrosal sinuses drain the cavernous sinus: the superior to the transverse/sigmoid sinus and the inferior to the IJV. Statement 2 is true: that is the main route of venous outflow from the brain, leaving the skull at the jugular foramen.

likely.t: Cavernous sinus: contents, drainage and thrombosis with CN VI as the first sign

stem:
A 23-year-old woman squeezed an infected pimple beside her nose 5 days ago.
Now: fever 39.4 °C, headache, swelling of both eyelids on the right and a bulging right eye.
Findings: her right eye can't move outward past the midline.
Which nerve is usually affected first in this condition, and why?
choices: CN VI, because it runs through the sinus beside the internal carotid artery
CN III, because it lies on the inside of the sinus beside the pituitary
CN IV, because it is the thinnest nerve in the sinus wall
V2, because it is the lowest nerve in the sinus wall
CN II, because it lies above the sinus
ex: Cavernous sinus thrombosis spreads from the danger triangle through the angular and ophthalmic veins (or from the teeth through the pterygoid plexus). CN VI lies free in the sinus beside the ICA, so the first nerve sign is usually loss of abduction; III, IV, V1 and V2 in the lateral wall follow.
why: Lying free in the sinus, unprotected by the wall, CN VI is usually hit first: the eye can't abduct.
CN III runs in the lateral wall, not free inside the sinus.
CN IV is thin but lies in the lateral wall; its loss affects downward gaze, not abduction.
V2 is sensory; it would cause cheek numbness, not a failure of abduction.
Severe swelling can reach CN II, but it is not the usual first sign and wouldn't stop abduction.

stem: True or false: The abducens nerve runs through the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery, while III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the lateral wall of the sinus.
ex: Inside the sinus: ICA (with its sympathetic plexus) and CN VI. Lateral wall, top to bottom: III, IV, V1, V2.
why: Both halves are right: VI and the ICA run through the sinus; III, IV, V1 and V2 are in its wall.
The statement is correct as written; no nerve is out of place.

stem:
Which structures pass through the jugular foramen?
1. Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
2. Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
3. Vagus nerve (CN X)
4. Accessory nerve (CN XI)
ex: The jugular foramen passes IX, X and XI along with the sigmoid sinus becoming the IJV. XII has its own hypoglossal canal just above the foramen magnum.
why: It includes 1, which is false: CN XII leaves through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen. It leaves out 4, which is true: CN XI enters through the foramen magnum and leaves through the jugular foramen.
It includes 1, which is false: CN XII leaves through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen.
It leaves out 4, which is true: CN XI enters through the foramen magnum and leaves through the jugular foramen.
Statements 2, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 1 is false: CN XII leaves through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen.

likely.t: Foramina of the skull and what passes through each (rotundum, ovale, spinosum, jugular foramen)

stem: Which statement about where cranial nerves leave the skull is false?
choices: V2 leaves through the foramen ovale
V3 leaves through the foramen ovale
CN VII and VIII enter the internal acoustic meatus
CN XI enters through the foramen magnum and leaves through the jugular foramen
ex: V1: superior orbital fissure; V2: foramen rotundum; V3: foramen ovale. VII and VIII: internal acoustic meatus (VII exits the base at the stylomastoid foramen). IX, X, XI: jugular foramen. XII: hypoglossal canal.
why: This is the false one: V2 leaves through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa; V3 uses the foramen ovale.
True: the mandibular nerve passes through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa.
True: both enter the meatus; VII then runs in the facial canal to the stylomastoid foramen.
True: its spinal roots climb through the foramen magnum and it leaves with IX and X.

stem:
A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation comes in 2 hours after his speech became slurred.
Findings: the right corner of his mouth droops and he can't smile on the right, but he wrinkles his forehead and closes both eyes normally. His right arm is weak.
Where is the lesion?
choices: Left cerebral cortex or its descending fibers (upper motor neuron)
Right facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
Right facial nerve inside the parotid gland
Left facial nerve in the internal acoustic meatus
ex: Upper motor neuron facial weakness (stroke) spares the forehead and affects the opposite lower face. Lower motor neuron weakness (Bell palsy, parotid tumor, a misplaced inferior alveolar injection into the parotid) paralyzes the whole same-side face.
why: The forehead gets cortical input from both sides, so a cortical lesion weakens only the opposite lower face, here with arm weakness from an MCA stroke.
A facial nerve (lower motor neuron) lesion paralyzes the whole same-side face, forehead included.
This would still paralyze the forehead (temporal branch) and wouldn't explain the arm weakness.
A left nerve lesion would weaken the left face, all of it, with hearing or taste changes.
V is sensory to the face and motor to chewing; it doesn't move the corner of the mouth.

likely.t: Cranial nerve lesions: III palsy, tongue and uvula deviation, UMN vs LMN facial weakness, corneal reflex

stem: A patient is asked to stick out his tongue. It deviates to the right, and the right side of the tongue is wasted and wrinkled. Which nerve is damaged?
ex: XII supplies all tongue muscles except the palatoglossus (X). With one XII cut, the opposite genioglossus is unopposed and pushes the protruded tongue toward the side of the lesion.
why: The lingual nerve is sensory (and carries chorda tympani fibers); it moves no tongue muscle.
The vagus supplies only the palatoglossus among tongue muscles; its lesion shows at the palate and uvula.
The intact left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak right side, and the right half wastes.
A left lesion would weaken the left genioglossus and push the tongue to the left.
IX is sensory and taste to the back third of the tongue; it doesn't protrude the tongue.

stem: True or false: In a patient with a right vagus nerve lesion, the uvula deviates to the right when the patient says "Ah."
ex: With the right vagus cut, the right side of the palate droops and the intact left levator veli palatini pulls the uvula toward the left, the healthy side.
why: The uvula deviates toward the normal side, so with a right lesion it points left.
The uvula moves away from the lesion, to the left here; the tongue is the one that deviates toward a lesion.

stem:
A 45-year-old woman keeps bumping into door frames.
History: headaches and irregular periods for a year.
Findings: she can't see objects in the outer half of the visual field of either eye.
MRI: a mass in the sella turcica pressing upward.
Which part of the visual pathway is compressed?
ex: The optic chiasm sits just above the sella. A pituitary adenoma presses the crossing nasal fibers from both eyes, which see the temporal visual fields, causing bitemporal hemianopia.
why: The crossing fibers from both nasal retinas, which see the temporal fields, are pressed by a pituitary adenoma: bitemporal hemianopia.
An optic nerve lesion blinds one eye completely.
A tract lesion takes away the same half of both visual fields on the opposite side (homonymous hemianopia).
CN III moves the eye and the pupil; it doesn't carry vision.
A cortical lesion also causes a homonymous field loss, usually sparing the macula.

likely.t: Visual pathway lesions and skull bones

stem:
A 50-year-old man has a sudden severe headache.
Findings: his left eyelid droops completely; lifting it shows a dilated pupil that doesn't react to light and an eye turned down and out.
Which lesion fits best?
choices: Compression of the left oculomotor nerve by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
ex: CN III supplies the levator palpebrae, four extraocular muscles and, through the ciliary ganglion, the sphincter pupillae. Its palsy: complete ptosis, dilated fixed pupil and an eye down and out (SO and LR unopposed). An aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery (or the PCA/superior cerebellar arteries it passes between) is a classic cause.
why: CN III passes next to the posterior communicating artery; pressure hits its outer parasympathetic fibers first (dilated pupil), then the muscles.
Horner gives a partial ptosis and a small pupil, the opposite of this pupil.
VI palsy leaves the eye turned in, with a normal lid and pupil.
IV palsy causes vertical double vision with the eye drifting up, not a full ptosis and dilated pupil.
VII closes the eye (orbicularis oculi); its loss leaves the eye open, not drooping shut.

stem: An 80-year-old man on warfarin fell against a cabinet 3 weeks ago. He now has slowly worsening confusion. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection over the left hemisphere that crosses the suture lines. What bled?
choices: Berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis
ex: Subdural hematoma: torn bridging veins, crescent shape, crosses sutures, often slow, in older people, people who drink heavily, or those on anticoagulants after minor trauma.
why: That bleeds into the subarachnoid space with a sudden, severe headache.
Cavernous sinus disease shows eye and cranial nerve signs, not a crescent over the hemisphere.
Veins crossing from the brain to the dural sinuses tear between dura and arachnoid; the slow venous bleed spreads as a crescent.
That bleed is epidural: lens-shaped, doesn't cross sutures, usually fast after a skull blow.

likely.t: Epidural vs subdural vs subarachnoid bleeds

stem: Each of the following is a bone of the neurocranium EXCEPT the:
ex: Neurocranium: frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, occipital (unpaired); parietal and temporal (paired). Viscerocranium: maxilla, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine, inferior concha, mandible and vomer.
why: Counted with the braincase: its cribriform plate forms part of the anterior fossa floor.
Unpaired bone of the braincase in the middle fossa.
Unpaired bone of the braincase around the foramen magnum.
The cheekbone is part of the facial skeleton (viscerocranium).
Unpaired bone of the braincase.

stem: A wisp of cotton touched to the patient's left cornea makes neither eye blink. Touching the right cornea makes both eyes blink, and the patient can close both eyes tightly on request. Which nerve is damaged?
ex: Corneal reflex: afferent V1 (nasociliary branches), efferent VII to the orbicularis oculi of both sides. No blink to one cornea, with a normal blink to the other cornea and normal eye closure, points to the afferent V1 on the silent side.
why: With the right VII cut, the right eye wouldn't blink to either stimulus.
The afferent limb from the left cornea is lost, so neither eye blinks to it, while both facial nerves still work.
If the left VII were cut, the left eye couldn't close tightly, and touching the right cornea would make only the right eye blink.
CN III raises the lid; it isn't part of the blink reflex arc.
Touch on the cornea is carried by V1, not by the optic nerve.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman has had slowly worsening hearing in her left ear and ringing for 2 years.
Now: unsteady walking, and she can't wrinkle the left side of her forehead.
The tumor most likely sits at which location?
ex: An acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) starts on CN VIII in the internal acoustic meatus: one-sided hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance. As it grows it compresses CN VII beside it.
why: A vestibular schwannoma of VIII grows here and presses on VII, which shares the meatus.
A tumor here affects IX, X and XI: hoarseness, trouble swallowing, weak shrug.
A lesion here weakens the face but spares hearing and balance.
A lesion here affects III, IV, V1 and VI around the eye.
A lesion here affects V3: jaw muscles and lower face sensation.

stem:
A 27-year-old man was punched in the right eye.
Chief complaint: double vision when he looks up.
Findings: the right eye can't elevate fully; the skin of the right cheek, side of the nose and upper lip is numb; the eye looks slightly sunken.
Which injury explains these findings?
choices: Fracture of the lateral wall with injury to the zygomatic nerve
Fracture of the orbital floor with entrapment of the inferior rectus and injury to the infraorbital nerve
Fracture of the orbital roof with injury to the frontal nerve
Compression of CN VI in the superior orbital fissure
Detachment of the levator palpebrae superioris
ex: A blow-out fracture most often breaks the orbital floor. The inferior rectus (and fat) gets trapped, so the eye can't look up, and the infraorbital nerve in the floor is injured, numbing the cheek, side of the nose and upper lip.
why: The lateral wall is strong, and the zygomatic nerve supplies a small patch of skin over the cheekbone and temple only.
The thin floor breaks into the maxillary sinus, catching the inferior rectus and the infraorbital nerve that runs in it.
A roof fracture numbs the forehead (frontal nerve), not the cheek, and doesn't trap the inferior rectus.
VI palsy stops abduction, not elevation, and causes no numbness.
That would cause a droopy lid, not double vision on upward gaze with cheek numbness.

likely.t: Orbit: blow-out fracture, extraocular muscle actions and nerves, accommodation and glaucoma

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers for the parotid gland reach it on the auriculotemporal nerve.
2. The facial nerve gives secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland as it passes through it.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Parotid secretion: IX → tympanic nerve → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve. The facial nerve only passes through.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: VII forms its plexus inside the parotid but supplies the gland with nothing; its secretory fibers go to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands.
Statement 1 is true, not false: after synapsing in the otic ganglion, the fibers from IX ride the auriculotemporal branch of V3 into the gland.

Statement 1 is true: after synapsing in the otic ganglion, the fibers from IX ride the auriculotemporal branch of V3 into the gland. Statement 2 is false: VII forms its plexus inside the parotid but supplies the gland with nothing; its secretory fibers go to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands.

Statement 1 is true, not false: after synapsing in the otic ganglion, the fibers from IX ride the auriculotemporal branch of V3 into the gland. Statement 2 is false, not true: VII forms its plexus inside the parotid but supplies the gland with nothing; its secretory fibers go to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands.

likely.t: Parotid: what runs through it, the duct opposite the maxillary second molar, IX–otic–auriculotemporal secretion, Frey syndrome

stem:
A 48-year-old woman had a benign tumor removed from her right parotid gland 9 months ago.
Chief complaint: "My right cheek gets sweaty and red whenever I eat."
What is the anatomical basis of this problem?
choices: Loss of the gland's sympathetic supply from the superior cervical ganglion
Blockage of the parotid duct by scar tissue
Cut parasympathetic fibers from the auriculotemporal nerve regrowing into the sweat glands of the skin
Injury to the marginal mandibular branch of VII
Injury to the great auricular nerve alone
ex: Frey syndrome (gustatory sweating): after parotid surgery or trauma, secretomotor fibers that ran on the auriculotemporal nerve regrow along cut skin nerves (great auricular, auriculotemporal) into sweat glands, so the thought or taste of food causes cheek sweating and flushing.
why: Loss of sympathetic supply would reduce, not cause, sweating.
A blocked duct gives painful swelling at meals, not sweating of the skin.
This is Frey syndrome: salivary signals now drive the sweat glands of the cheek.
That branch moves the lower lip; its injury weakens the smile, not sweating.
Great auricular injury numbs the skin over the gland and ear lobe; on its own it doesn't cause sweating.

likely.t: Parotid: what runs through it, the duct opposite the maxillary second molar, IX–otic–auriculotemporal secretion, Frey syndrome

stem: True or false: The parotid duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the maxillary second molar.
ex: The duct crosses the masseter, pierces the buccinator and opens at the parotid papilla on the cheek opposite the maxillary second molar.
why: The parotid papilla is opposite the maxillary second molar, as stated.
The statement is correct: the submandibular duct is the one that opens under the tongue.

stem: Which statement about structures inside the parotid gland is true?
choices: The facial nerve is the most superficial of the structures passing through the gland
The external carotid artery lies superficial to the facial nerve in the gland
The retromandibular vein forms below the gland and enters it from beneath
The parotid sheath is an upward extension of the pretracheal fascia
ex: Through the parotid, from superficial to deep: facial nerve plexus, retromandibular vein, external carotid artery (which ends there as the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries). The sheath is investing fascia.
why: Superficial to deep: facial nerve, retromandibular vein, external carotid artery.
The ECA is the deepest of the three; the facial nerve is the most superficial.
It forms inside the gland from the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.
The sheath comes from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.

stem:
A 30-year-old patient receives an inferior alveolar nerve block. Within minutes she can't close her left eye and the left corner of her mouth droops. The lip and tongue are not yet numb.
What most likely happened?
choices: The anesthetic entered the pterygoid plexus
The needle went too far superiorly into the mandibular notch
The needle went too far posteriorly, into the parotid gland, anesthetizing the facial nerve
The needle was too low and anesthetized the lingual nerve
The needle injured the medial pterygoid muscle
ex: If the needle passes behind the ramus into the parotid gland, the anesthetic blocks the facial nerve plexus: temporary paralysis of the same-side face, with the eye unable to close. Protect the eye and reassure; it resolves as the drug wears off.
why: Intravascular injection risks a systemic reaction or hematoma, not facial paralysis.
This could reach the masseteric nerve, not the facial nerve branches.
Anesthetic deposited in the parotid reaches the facial plexus: a temporary Bell-like palsy that wears off with the drug.
Lingual anesthesia numbs the tongue; it doesn't paralyze face muscles.
Injury to the medial pterygoid causes trismus later, not facial paralysis.

likely.t: Facial nerve branches, Bell palsy and facial paralysis from a misplaced inferior alveolar block

stem: A patient with a right trochlear nerve palsy has trouble reading and walking down stairs. Which movement is weakest in the right eye?
ex: The superior oblique (IV) intorts, depresses and abducts the eye; it is tested by asking the patient to look down and in, where it is the main depressor. Its palsy causes vertical double vision when reading or going down stairs.
why: That is the superior rectus (III).
In adduction the superior oblique is the main depressor, so its loss shows when looking down and in.
Abduction is mainly the lateral rectus (VI).
Adduction is the medial rectus (III).
That is the inferior oblique (III).

stem: When the eye focuses on a book held close, what happens?
choices: The dilator pupillae contracts under sympathetic control
The ciliary muscle contracts through sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion
The lens becomes thinner as the zonular fibers are stretched
The ciliary muscle contracts, the zonular fibers relax and the lens rounds up
The ciliary muscle relaxes, the zonular fibers tighten and the lens flattens
ex: Accommodation: CN III fibers synapse in the ciliary ganglion; short ciliary nerves contract the ciliary muscle, which slackens the zonular fibers so the lens rounds up. The pupils also constrict and the eyes converge.
why: For near work the pupil constricts (parasympathetic), it doesn't dilate.
The ciliary muscle is driven by parasympathetic fibers of III.
Stretched zonules flatten the lens, which is the far-vision state.
Parasympathetic fibers from the ciliary ganglion contract the ciliary muscle, the zonules slacken and the elastic lens thickens.
That is the state for distant vision.

stem: A 60-year-old patient has open-angle glaucoma. Where is the main site of resistance to the outflow of aqueous humor?
choices: The trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm at the iridocorneal angle
ex: Aqueous humor: ciliary processes → posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork → canal of Schlemm → episcleral veins. When outflow is blocked, intraocular pressure rises and damages the optic nerve.
why: It drains the retina, not the aqueous humor.
Aqueous leaves the anterior chamber here into the veins; blockage raises intraocular pressure.
They produce aqueous humor; they are not the drainage route.
It drains tears into the inferior meatus, not fluid from inside the eye.
The vitreous fills the back of the eye; aqueous humor doesn't drain through it.

stem: A cyclist has a deep scalp laceration with a collection of pus that spreads freely across the top of the head. Which scalp layer is involved, and why is it dangerous?
choices: The dense connective tissue, because its vessels stay open when cut
The pericranium, because it is continuous with the dura through the sutures
The loose connective tissue, because emissary veins cross it to the dural sinuses
The skin, because its hair follicles connect directly to the dural sinuses
The aponeurosis, because it contains the scalp arteries
ex: Scalp layers: skin, dense connective tissue (vessels held open, so wounds bleed freely), aponeurosis, loose connective tissue (the danger zone: blood and pus spread, emissary veins lead to the dural sinuses) and pericranium.
why: This layer explains heavy bleeding, but its tight fibers keep infection local.
Infection under the pericranium is limited to one bone by the sutures.
This "danger zone" lets pus spread and drains through emissary veins into the skull.
The skin is not where infection spreads widely, and its follicles don't connect to the sinuses.
The aponeurosis is tendon; the scalp arteries run in the dense connective tissue above it.

likely.t: Sensory supply of the face, scalp layers and lacrimal secretion

stem: Each of the following is supplied by the facial nerve EXCEPT the:
ex: VII closes the eye (orbicularis oculi); III opens it (levator palpebrae superioris), with help from the sympathetic superior tarsal muscle.
why: Supplied by the cervical branch of VII.
Supplied by the temporal and zygomatic branches of VII; it closes the eye.
Supplied by VII just after it leaves the stylomastoid foramen.
It raises the eyelid and is supplied by the superior division of CN III.
A muscle of facial expression (arch 2), supplied by the buccal branches of VII.

likely.t: Facial nerve branches, Bell palsy and facial paralysis from a misplaced inferior alveolar block

stem: A tumor in the middle cranial fossa injures the greater petrosal nerve. Which problem is expected on that side?
choices: A dry mouth from loss of parotid secretion
A dry eye from loss of lacrimal secretion
Loss of taste on the front of the tongue
Paralysis of the muscles of facial expression
ex: Lacrimal secretion: VII → greater petrosal nerve → nerve of the pterygoid canal (joined by the deep petrosal) → pterygopalatine ganglion → zygomatic nerve (V2) → lacrimal nerve (V1) → gland. Loss gives a dry eye; it also dries the nasal and palatal glands.
why: The parotid gets its secretory fibers from IX through the lesser petrosal nerve.
The greater petrosal carries presynaptic fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion, which drives the lacrimal gland.
Taste from the front of the tongue travels in the chorda tympani, a separate branch of VII.
Pupil constriction depends on III and the ciliary ganglion.
The motor fibers stay in the facial canal to the stylomastoid foramen.

stem: Shingles vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) warn that the eye may be involved. Which nerve explains this link?
ex: The nasociliary nerve gives the long ciliary nerves (cornea) and, through the anterior ethmoidal nerve, the external nasal branch to the tip of the nose. Zoster on the nose tip means this branch, and likely the eye, is involved.
why: Its external nasal branch supplies the tip of the nose and its ciliary branches supply the cornea, so both are in one territory.
It supplies the side of the nose, not the tip, and has no branches to the eyeball.
It supplies the forehead near the midline, not the nose tip.
It is a motor branch to the orbicularis oculi with no skin sensation.
It supplies the lacrimal gland and the skin of the outer upper lid.

stem:
A 78-year-old woman has worn a complete lower denture for 25 years.
Chief complaint: sharp, shooting pain in her lower lip and chin when she chews.
Findings: a tender spot on the crest of the severely resorbed ridge in the premolar area.
What is the likely cause?
choices: Pressure on the long buccal nerve
Pressure on the mental nerve where the mental foramen now opens on the ridge crest
Pressure on the lingual nerve at the third molar area
Pressure on the nerve to the mylohyoid
ex: The mental foramen sits below the mandibular second premolar. After tooth loss and resorption of the alveolar process, the foramen (and even the mandibular canal) can come to lie on the crest, where a denture presses on the mental nerve. Relieve the denture over it.
why: The buccal nerve supplies the cheek and buccal gingiva of the molars, not the lip and chin.
V2 supplies the upper lip and cheek, not the lower lip and chin.
With the ridge resorbed, the foramen below the second premolar comes to the top of the bone, under the denture.
The lingual nerve supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth, not the chin and lower lip, and lies far behind the premolars.
This is a motor nerve on the inner surface of the mandible; it doesn't supply the lip or chin.

stem:
A 58-year-old man has a tumor at the left foramen ovale.
Findings: the left temple and the area over the left masseter look hollow; when he opens wide, his chin swings to one side.
Which way does the jaw deviate, and why?
choices: To the right, because the left temporalis is weak
To the left, because the right lateral pterygoid is unopposed
To the right, because the left medial pterygoid pulls it
Straight down, because the digastric opens the jaw by itself
To the left, because the right masseter is in spasm
ex: With one V3 cut, the opposite lateral pterygoid still pulls its condyle forward while the paralyzed side stays back, so the chin deviates toward the side of the lesion. The masseter and temporalis on that side waste.
why: The temporalis closes and retracts; its weakness doesn't steer the opening jaw.
The working right lateral pterygoid pulls the right condyle forward, swinging the chin toward the paralyzed left side.
The medial pterygoid is a closer; and the left one is the paralyzed side.
The digastric helps opening but can't make up for one lateral pterygoid; the jaw deviates.
Masseter spasm causes trismus, not deviation on opening.

likely.t: Muscles of mastication: actions, the lateral pterygoid as the opener, jaw deviation toward a V3 lesion

stem: During wide opening, which muscle pulls the condyle and the articular disc forward onto the articular eminence?
ex: The lateral pterygoid is the protruder and the only muscle of mastication that opens the jaw. Its pull glides the condyle and disc forward in the superior compartment during wide opening.
why: Its inferior head pulls the condylar neck forward and its superior head attaches to the disc and capsule.
It elevates and protrudes the jaw; it doesn't attach to the disc.
Its posterior fibers retract the condyle; it closes the jaw.
It is a strong elevator.
It helps depress the mandible from below but doesn't move the condyle forward.

likely.t: Muscles of mastication: actions, the lateral pterygoid as the opener, jaw deviation toward a V3 lesion

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The temporalis inserts on the condylar process and is the main protruder of the mandible.
2. Rotation (the hinge movement) of the TMJ occurs in the superior compartment, between the disc and the articular eminence.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Temporalis: coronoid process, elevates and retracts. TMJ: hinge in the inferior compartment, gliding (translation) in the superior compartment.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: the temporalis inserts on the coronoid process; it elevates, and its posterior fibers retract, while the lateral pterygoid protrudes. Statement 2 is false, not true: rotation happens in the inferior compartment, between the condyle and the disc; the superior compartment is where gliding happens.

Statement 1 is false: the temporalis inserts on the coronoid process; it elevates, and its posterior fibers retract, while the lateral pterygoid protrudes. Statement 2 is false: rotation happens in the inferior compartment, between the condyle and the disc; the superior compartment is where gliding happens.
Statement 1 is false, not true: the temporalis inserts on the coronoid process; it elevates, and its posterior fibers retract, while the lateral pterygoid protrudes.
Statement 2 is false, not true: rotation happens in the inferior compartment, between the condyle and the disc; the superior compartment is where gliding happens.

stem: True or false: The buccal nerve, the sensory branch of the anterior division of V3, supplies the cheek mucosa and the buccal gingiva of the mandibular molars.
ex: The buccal nerve is the one sensory branch of the mostly motor anterior division. An inferior alveolar block doesn't reach it, so the buccal gingiva of the molars needs a separate buccal injection.
why: This is the buccal branch of V3, as stated; it is separate from the motor buccal branches of VII.
The statement is correct: the buccal nerve is sensory and comes from the anterior division of V3.

likely.t: V3 branches, the chorda tympani on the lingual nerve, and the anatomy and complications of dental blocks

stem:
Which nerves are branches of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve?
1. Auriculotemporal nerve
2. Masseteric nerve
3. Inferior alveolar nerve
4. Lingual nerve
ex: Posterior division (mostly sensory): auriculotemporal, lingual and inferior alveolar (with the motor nerve to the mylohyoid). Anterior division (mostly motor): masseteric, deep temporal, lateral pterygoid and the sensory buccal nerve.
why: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: the masseteric nerve is a motor branch of the anterior division; it reaches the masseter through the mandibular notch.
It leaves out 3, which is true: the inferior alveolar nerve is the largest branch of the posterior division.

It includes 2, which is false: the masseteric nerve is a motor branch of the anterior division; it reaches the masseter through the mandibular notch. It leaves out 1, which is true: the auriculotemporal nerve arises from the posterior division by two roots around the middle meningeal artery.
It leaves out 1, which is true: the auriculotemporal nerve arises from the posterior division by two roots around the middle meningeal artery.

likely.t: V3 branches, the chorda tympani on the lingual nerve, and the anatomy and complications of dental blocks

stem: Which statement about the maxillary artery is false?
choices: The masseteric and deep temporal arteries come from its second part
The middle meningeal artery comes from its third part
The inferior alveolar artery comes from its first part
The posterior superior alveolar artery comes from its third part
ex: First part: middle meningeal, inferior alveolar (and small ear branches). Second part: muscular branches and buccal. Third part: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, descending palatine, artery of the pterygoid canal, pharyngeal, sphenopalatine.
why: True: the second (pterygoid) part supplies the muscles of mastication.
This is the false one: the middle meningeal artery comes from the first part, behind the condylar neck.
True: the first (mandibular) part gives the inferior alveolar artery to the mandibular teeth.
True: the third part, in the pterygopalatine fossa, gives the posterior superior alveolar artery.

likely.t: Maxillary artery parts and fossa boundaries

stem:
A 34-year-old patient receives a posterior superior alveolar block for a maxillary second molar.
Within a minute: the right cheek and the area below the eye swell rapidly and turn bluish.
What was most likely injured?
ex: The PSA injection site lies at the back of the maxillary tuberosity, next to the pterygoid plexus (and the maxillary artery). A needle placed too deep can puncture them, causing a fast hematoma. Apply pressure and cold.
why: Injury to the duct doesn't cause rapid bluish swelling.
Nerve injury causes numbness or tingling, not a fast swelling.
Overinserting the needle behind the tuberosity enters the plexus, and bleeding into the infratemporal fossa spreads into the cheek.
The facial artery runs across the mandible and up the face, far from the PSA injection site.
The lingual artery is deep in the floor of the mouth.

stem: During an inferior alveolar block, the anesthetic is deposited near the mandibular foramen. Which structure attaches to the lingula, lies medial to the nerve and can block the spread of the solution if the needle is too medial?
ex: The sphenomandibular ligament (a Meckel's cartilage remnant) passes from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula. The inferior alveolar nerve enters the foramen lateral to it, in the pterygomandibular space between the ramus and the medial pterygoid.
why: It runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula, medial to the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels.
It runs from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible, below and behind the foramen.
The raphe is a landmark the needle passes lateral to, joining the buccinator and superior constrictor.
It reinforces the side of the TMJ capsule, far above the foramen.
It runs from the styloid process to the hyoid, an arch 2 remnant away from the foramen.

stem:
A 25-year-old woman had two inferior alveolar blocks on the right 3 days ago for a difficult restoration.
Chief complaint: pain and trouble opening her mouth.
Findings: maximum opening 18 mm; no swelling of the face; no fever.
Which muscle was most likely injured by the needle?
ex: Trismus after an inferior alveolar block is usually from trauma or a small hematoma in the medial pterygoid, which lines the injection space. Heat, gentle opening exercises and pain relief help.
why: The temporalis inserts on the coronoid process, but the IANB needle goes into the pterygomandibular space below it.
It lies above the injection site; injury to it would limit opening less directly.
The needle passes through it, but its injury doesn't limit opening.
It forms the medial wall of the pterygomandibular space; a needle into it, or bleeding in it, leads to trismus.
The needle stays medial to the ramus; the masseter lies on its lateral side.

stem: After removal of an impacted mandibular third molar, a patient has lost general sensation and taste on the front two-thirds of the left side of the tongue. Which nerve was injured?
ex: The lingual nerve runs close to the lingual cortex beside the mandibular third molar. Below where the chorda tympani joins it, it carries general sensation (V3) and taste (VII) from the front two-thirds of the tongue, plus secretomotor fibers for the submandibular ganglion.
why: Its injury numbs the lower teeth, lip and chin, not the tongue.
It lies against the lingual plate near the third molar and carries both its own general sensation and the chorda tympani's taste fibers.
XII is motor; it doesn't carry sensation or taste.
IX supplies the back third of the tongue.
This motor nerve supplies the mylohyoid and anterior digastric.

stem:
A 40-year-old man yawned widely and can't close his mouth.
Findings: the mouth is fixed open, both sides of the face are tense, and there is a hollow in front of each ear.
Where are the condyles?
choices: Pushed up into the middle cranial fossa
Medial to the spine of the sphenoid
In front of the articular eminence
Still in the mandibular fossa, with the disc torn out
ex: TMJ dislocation is nearly always anterior (often both sides): the condyle passes in front of the articular eminence and the elevators spasm. Reduce by pressing down on the molars, then pushing back.
why: That needs a hard blow under the chin; it doesn't follow a yawn.
The spine of the sphenoid helps stop medial displacement.
In a wide yawn the condyle slides over and in front of the eminence, and muscle spasm keeps it there.
Posterior dislocation is rare because of the postglenoid tubercle and the lateral ligament.
A displaced disc can lock the jaw closed or click, but it doesn't leave a hollow in front of the ear.

likely.t: TMJ structure, compartments, dislocation and nerve supply

stem: Each of the following is a branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) EXCEPT the:
ex: V3 branches: buccal, masseteric, deep temporal, lateral and medial pterygoid nerves, auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar (nerve to the mylohyoid, mental, incisive). The superior alveolar nerves belong to V2.
why: A branch of the posterior division of V3.
A branch of the posterior division of V3.
A motor branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3).
It comes off V2 in the pterygopalatine fossa to supply the maxillary molars.
A sensory branch of the anterior division of V3.

stem: Which feature of the TMJ is unusual among synovial joints?
choices: Its articular surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage instead of hyaline cartilage
Its disc is richly supplied with blood vessels in the area that bears load
It is supplied only by the facial nerve
ex: The TMJ is a synovial joint whose articular surfaces and disc are fibrocartilage. The disc divides it into a superior (gliding) and inferior (hinge) compartment. Nerves: auriculotemporal and masseteric.
why: Dense fibrous tissue covers the condyle and the eminence, adapted to the joint's load and remodeling.
It has a fibrous capsule lined by synovial membrane.
The load-bearing center of the disc is avascular; the vessels are in the retrodiscal tissue.
Its main nerve is the auriculotemporal (V3), with the masseteric nerve.
It hinges in the inferior compartment and glides in the superior compartment.

stem: A patient with a painful clicking TMJ also complains of earache, though the ear exam is normal. Which nerve best explains why the pain is felt in the ear?
ex: The auriculotemporal nerve is the main sensory nerve of the TMJ and also supplies the external acoustic meatus and outer surface of the tympanic membrane, so TMJ disorders often present as ear pain.
why: It supplies the TMJ and also the external acoustic meatus and the outer tympanic membrane, so joint pain is felt in the ear.
It crosses the middle ear but carries taste and secretomotor fibers, not pain from the joint.
It supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and the ear lobe, not the joint.
It carries parasympathetic fibers for the parotid, not sensation.
It is a motor branch of VII.

stem: True or false: The infratemporal crest of the greater wing of the sphenoid separates the infratemporal fossa from the pterygopalatine fossa.
ex: The infratemporal crest separates the temporal fossa above from the infratemporal fossa below. The infratemporal fossa opens into the pterygopalatine fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure.
why: The crest divides the temporal fossa from the infratemporal fossa, not from the pterygopalatine fossa.
The pterygopalatine fossa is reached through the pterygomaxillary fissure; the crest is the line between the temporal and infratemporal fossae.

stem: The stapedius, the stylohyoid and the posterior belly of the digastric come from the same pharyngeal arch. Which arch, and which nerve supplies them?
ex: A muscle keeps the nerve of its arch: arch 2 muscles (facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric) are all supplied by VII.
why: Arch 3 makes only one muscle, the stylopharyngeus.
Arch 4 makes the cricothyroid, constrictors and palate muscles.
Arch 2 (Reichert's cartilage) gives the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid and posterior digastric, all VII.
Arch 1 muscles are the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.
Arch 6 makes the intrinsic laryngeal muscles other than the cricothyroid.

likely.t: Pharyngeal arch nerves and derivatives, and pouch derivatives

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus both develop from the third pharyngeal pouch.
2. The superior parathyroid glands develop from the second pharyngeal pouch.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Pouch 1: tympanic cavity and auditory tube. Pouch 2: palatine tonsil lining. Pouch 3: inferior parathyroid and thymus. Pouch 4: superior parathyroid and ultimobranchial body (C cells).
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: the superior parathyroids come from pouch 4; pouch 2 lines the palatine tonsil.
Statement 1 is true, not false: the dorsal part of pouch 3 gives the inferior parathyroid and the ventral part the thymus, which drags the gland down below the pouch 4 gland.

Statement 1 is true: the dorsal part of pouch 3 gives the inferior parathyroid and the ventral part the thymus, which drags the gland down below the pouch 4 gland. Statement 2 is false: the superior parathyroids come from pouch 4; pouch 2 lines the palatine tonsil.

Statement 1 is true, not false: the dorsal part of pouch 3 gives the inferior parathyroid and the ventral part the thymus, which drags the gland down below the pouch 4 gland. Statement 2 is false, not true: the superior parathyroids come from pouch 4; pouch 2 lines the palatine tonsil.

likely.t: Pharyngeal arch nerves and derivatives, and pouch derivatives

stem:
A 20-year-old man has a painless swelling on the right side of his neck that has slowly grown over a year.
Findings: a soft, smooth, 3-cm mass along the anterior border of the SCM at the level of the hyoid; it doesn't move when he swallows or sticks out his tongue.
What is the most likely origin of this mass?
choices: A remnant of the first pharyngeal membrane
A cystic thymus remnant from pouch 3
ex: Arch 2 grows down over grooves 2–4, pinching them into the cervical sinus. If it persists, it forms a lateral cervical cyst or fistula along the anterior border of the SCM. A thyroglossal duct cyst is midline and moves with the tongue.
why: A lateral cervical (branchial) cyst lies along the anterior border of the SCM and often shows up in young adults.
A thyroglossal duct cyst is in or near the midline and moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion.
Parathyroid tissue is tiny and usually found near the thyroid, not as a soft lateral cyst.
The first membrane becomes the tympanic membrane.
Thymic remnants are rare and usually lower in the neck or chest; this is not the classic lateral cyst.

likely.t: Clefts, tongue development and neck cysts

stem: True or false: A thyroglossal duct cyst lies in or near the midline of the neck and moves upward when the patient sticks out the tongue.
ex: The thyroid descends from the foramen cecum of the tongue along the thyroglossal duct, in front of the hyoid. A leftover piece forms a midline cyst attached toward the tongue and hyoid, so it rises with swallowing and tongue protrusion.
why: Midline position and movement with the tongue are the signs that set it apart from a lateral cervical cyst.
The statement is correct; it is the lateral cervical cyst that sits off the midline along the SCM.

stem: A newborn has a cleft of the left upper lip that runs back through the alveolar ridge between the lateral incisor and canine, ending at the incisive foramen; the palate behind the foramen is intact. Failure of which fusion caused this?
choices: The two medial nasal prominences with each other
The maxillary prominence with the lateral nasal prominence
The two mandibular prominences with each other
The left maxillary prominence with the intermaxillary segment
The two palatine shelves with each other
ex: The intermaxillary segment (merged medial nasal prominences) makes the philtrum, premaxilla and primary palate. When a maxillary prominence fails to fuse with it, the result is an anterior cleft: cleft lip, which can extend through the alveolus (between the lateral incisor and canine) to the incisive foramen.
why: That causes a rare median cleft lip.
That causes an oblique facial cleft exposing the nasolacrimal duct.
Those fuse early and very rarely fail; a cleft there is in the lower lip and jaw.
This anterior cleft can involve the lip, the alveolus and the primary palate up to the incisive foramen.
That causes a posterior cleft palate, behind the incisive foramen.

stem: Why is the posterior third of the tongue supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, while the anterior two-thirds get general sensation from V3?
choices: The posterior third comes from the hypopharyngeal eminence over arches 3 and 4
The posterior third comes from occipital myotomes
The anterior two-thirds come from the copula of arch 2
The posterior third forms around the foramen cecum from the thyroid diverticulum
The anterior two-thirds come from the tuberculum impar alone
ex: Front two-thirds: lateral lingual swellings of arch 1, general sensation V3 (lingual nerve), taste VII (chorda tympani). Back third: hypopharyngeal eminence of arches 3 and 4, sensation and taste IX (X at the base). Muscles: occipital myotomes, XII.
why: A region keeps the nerves of the arches it came from: arch 3 (IX) and arch 4 (X) behind, arch 1 (V3) in front.
The myotomes form the tongue muscles (XII), not its lining.
The copula is overgrown and doesn't form the adult tongue; the front comes from arch 1.
The thyroid diverticulum leaves the tongue; it doesn't form its back third.
The tuberculum impar is overgrown by the lateral lingual swellings and adds little to the adult tongue.

stem: Which statement about the nerve supply of the pharynx is true?
choices: The sensory limb of the gag reflex is carried mainly by the vagus
The stylopharyngeus is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by IX
The superior constrictor is supplied by IX through the pharyngeal plexus
The pharyngeal plexus lies mainly on the inferior constrictor
ex: Pharyngeal muscles: all X through the pharyngeal plexus (on the middle constrictor), except the stylopharyngeus (IX). Gag reflex: IX in, X out.
why: The oropharynx touched in a gag test is supplied by IX; the vagus is the motor limb.
It is the single arch 3 muscle; every other pharyngeal muscle is X.
All three constrictors are supplied by the vagus through the plexus.
The plexus lies mainly on the middle constrictor.

likely.t: Pharynx: all X except the stylopharyngeus, gag reflex, piriform recess and tonsillar bed

stem:
A 45-year-old woman had a fish bone removed from her right piriform recess.
Now: food and liquid go "down the wrong way" without making her cough.
Which nerve was most likely injured?
ex: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and runs under the mucosa of the piriform recess. Damage there numbs the laryngeal vestibule, so food can enter the larynx without the protective cough.
why: It is motor to the cricothyroid; its loss changes pitch.
IX supplies the oropharynx; the piriform recess is in the laryngopharynx.
It runs under the mucosa of the piriform recess and is sensory to the larynx above the vocal folds, the trigger of the cough reflex.
Its injury causes hoarseness; it supplies sensation below the vocal folds, not the vestibule.
XII moves the tongue; it carries no sensation from the larynx.

stem: Two weeks after a tonsillectomy, a patient says food tastes "flat" at the back of the tongue, and that area feels numb. Which nerve, lying on the tonsillar bed, was affected?
ex: The tonsillar bed is the superior constrictor between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. IX lies on it, so swelling or injury after tonsillectomy can dull taste and sensation on the back third of the tongue. Bleeding comes from the tonsillar branch of the facial artery and the external palatine vein.
why: IX runs on the superior constrictor in the tonsillar bed and supplies taste and sensation to the back third of the tongue.
It supplies the front two-thirds of the tongue and lies in the floor of the mouth, not on the tonsillar bed.
It carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue.
XII is motor; its injury would weaken the tongue.
It supplies the larynx above the vocal folds and the epiglottic region, below the tonsil.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman has a total thyroidectomy for cancer.
In recovery: noisy, high-pitched breathing (stridor) and shortness of breath; her voice is weak.
Laryngoscopy: both vocal folds sit near the midline and don't move apart on inspiration.
Loss of which muscle best explains the airway problem?
ex: Both recurrent laryngeal nerves can be injured near the inferior thyroid arteries. All intrinsic muscles but the cricothyroid are lost, including the only abductor, the posterior cricoarytenoid, so both folds stay near the midline: stridor that may need an airway. One nerve alone causes hoarseness.
why: It adducts the folds; losing it would not close the airway.
It adducts the back of the folds.
It relaxes the folds.
It is the only abductor; with both recurrent laryngeal nerves cut, neither side can open the rima glottidis.
It tenses the folds; it is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve and doesn't open the airway.

likely.t: Larynx: posterior cricoarytenoid as the only abductor, cricothyroid on the external laryngeal nerve, RLN injury, cricothyrotomy

stem: True or false: The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
ex: The cricothyroid (arch 4) is supplied by the external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; every other intrinsic laryngeal muscle (arch 6) is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
why: The cricothyroid is the one exception to the recurrent laryngeal rule.
The external laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid; the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the rest.

stem: A diner chokes on a large piece of meat. The Heimlich maneuver fails and he can't be intubated. An emergency airway is made through the midline of the neck just below the thyroid cartilage. Which structure is cut?
ex: Cricothyrotomy: skin, fascia and the median cricothyroid ligament (part of the conus elasticus), between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, below the level of the vocal folds.
why: Tracheostomy goes through the rings, lower down, and is not the fast emergency route.
The isthmus lies over rings 2–4; cutting it bleeds and is avoided in an emergency.
It joins the thyroid and cricoid cartilages in the midline, just under the skin, below the vocal folds.
It lies above the thyroid cartilage, above the vocal folds and the obstruction.
It lies inside the larynx; cutting it would not open an airway.

stem: Each of the following develops from the first pharyngeal arch EXCEPT the:
ex: Arch 1: malleus, incus, sphenomandibular ligament; muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini. Arch 2: stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, upper hyoid.
why: Arch 1, from the dorsal end of the first arch cartilage.
Arch 1 muscle, supplied by V3.
Arch 1 muscle, supplied by the nerve to the mylohyoid (V3).
Arch 2, from Reichert's cartilage, like the stapedius that moves it.
Arch 1, from Meckel's cartilage.

stem: A 33-year-old man with a new left Bell palsy also says ordinary sounds, such as dishes clattering, are painfully loud in his left ear. Paralysis of which muscle explains this?
ex: The nerve to the stapedius leaves VII in the facial canal. A lesion above that branch (as in many cases of Bell palsy) paralyzes the stapedius and causes hyperacusis. The tensor tympani (V3) is spared.
why: It opens the auditory tube; it doesn't damp the ossicles.
Supplied by VII inside the facial canal, it damps the stapes; without it, normal sound feels too loud (hyperacusis).
It also damps sound but is supplied by V3, which is intact here.
It lifts the pharynx and helps open the auditory tube.
An outer ear muscle with no effect on hearing.

likely.t: Ear: stapedius and hyperacusis, middle ear walls and the spread of infection

stem: A child with untreated chronic otitis media develops fever, headache and confusion. CT shows the infection has eroded the roof of the middle ear (tegmen tympani). Into which region has it spread?
ex: Middle ear walls: roof (tegmen tympani, middle cranial fossa), floor (jugular bulb), anterior (carotid canal, auditory tube), posterior (mastoid antrum and air cells), medial (inner ear, promontory), lateral (tympanic membrane).
why: The tegmen tympani is the thin roof between the middle ear and the temporal lobe in the middle cranial fossa: meningitis or a temporal lobe abscess.
The floor of the middle ear separates it from the jugular bulb; this infection went through the roof.
These open through the posterior wall (the mastoid antrum).
The anterior (carotid) wall separates the middle ear from the carotid canal.
Spread through the medial wall causes labyrinthitis.

stem:
Which pairings of a pterygopalatine fossa opening and the region it connects to are correct?
1. Foramen rotundum: middle cranial fossa
2. Sphenopalatine foramen: oral cavity
3. Pterygomaxillary fissure: infratemporal fossa
4. Greater palatine canal: nasopharynx
ex: Rotundum to the middle cranial fossa (V2), sphenopalatine foramen to the nasal cavity, pterygomaxillary fissure to the infratemporal fossa, inferior orbital fissure to the orbit, palatine canals to the palate, palatovaginal canal to the nasopharynx.
why: It includes 2, which is false: the sphenopalatine foramen opens into the nasal cavity, not the mouth.

Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false: the sphenopalatine foramen opens into the nasal cavity, not the mouth. Statement 4 is false: the greater palatine canal leads down to the hard palate; the nasopharynx is reached by the palatovaginal canal.
It includes 4, which is false: the greater palatine canal leads down to the hard palate; the nasopharynx is reached by the palatovaginal canal.

It includes 4, which is false: the greater palatine canal leads down to the hard palate; the nasopharynx is reached by the palatovaginal canal. It leaves out 1, which is true: V2 enters the fossa from the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum.

likely.t: Pterygopalatine fossa openings and its ganglion

stem: Which statement about the pterygopalatine ganglion is false?
choices: Its postganglionic fibers drive the lacrimal, nasal and palatal glands
Sensory fibers of V2 pass through it without synapsing
Sympathetic fibers of the deep petrosal nerve synapse in it
Presynaptic parasympathetic fibers of the greater petrosal nerve synapse in it
ex: The nerve of the pterygoid canal brings the greater petrosal (presynaptic parasympathetic) and deep petrosal (postsynaptic sympathetic) nerves to the ganglion. Only the parasympathetic fibers synapse; sympathetic and V2 sensory fibers pass straight through.
why: True: they reach the glands on branches of V2 (and V1 for the lacrimal gland).
True: the sensory cell bodies are in the trigeminal ganglion.
This is the false one: they are already postganglionic (from the superior cervical ganglion) and pass through without synapsing.
True: these VII fibers are the only ones that synapse in the ganglion.

stem: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension has heavy bleeding from the back of his nose that runs down his throat; packing the front of the nose doesn't stop it. Which artery is the most likely source?
ex: Most nosebleeds come from Kiesselbach's area on the anterior septum (sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine and superior labial branches). Posterior bleeds, common in older hypertensive patients, come from the sphenopalatine artery.
why: It supplies the upper front of the nasal cavity.
The main artery of the nasal cavity enters at the back through the sphenopalatine foramen and is the usual source of posterior nosebleeds.
Its septal branch bleeds from the front of the septum, which anterior packing controls.
It runs in the orbital floor to the face, not into the nose.
It supplies the tongue.

likely.t: Maxillary sinus drainage and the teeth; nosebleeds and nasal drainage

stem:
A maxillary first molar with long roots is extracted.
One week later: the patient says water comes out of his nose when he drinks, and air bubbles from the socket when he blows his nose.
The opening leads into a sinus that normally drains through which opening?
choices: Semilunar hiatus of the middle meatus
ex: The roots of the maxillary molars and premolars sit just under the floor of the maxillary sinus, so an extraction can leave an oroantral communication. The sinus drains to the semilunar hiatus in the middle meatus from high on its medial wall, which is why it drains poorly and is infected most often.
why: Only the nasolacrimal duct opens there.
That drains the posterior ethmoidal cells.
No sinus drains straight into the nasopharynx.
The maxillary sinus drains here, through an ostium high on its medial wall.
That drains the sphenoid sinus.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The nasolacrimal duct opens into the middle meatus.
2. The sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess, above the superior concha.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Sphenoethmoidal recess: sphenoid sinus. Superior meatus: posterior ethmoidal cells. Middle meatus: frontal, maxillary, anterior and middle ethmoidal. Inferior meatus: nasolacrimal duct.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus, under the inferior concha.
Statement 2 is true, not false: the sphenoid sinus opens through its front wall into the recess above the superior concha.

Statement 1 is false, not true: the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus, under the inferior concha. Statement 2 is true, not false: the sphenoid sinus opens through its front wall into the recess above the superior concha.

Statement 1 is false: the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus, under the inferior concha. Statement 2 is true: the sphenoid sinus opens through its front wall into the recess above the superior concha.

stem: After middle ear surgery, a 40-year-old woman has lost taste on the front two-thirds of the left side of her tongue. Touch and temperature there feel normal, and her face moves normally. Which nerve was injured?
choices: Facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
ex: The chorda tympani leaves VII in the facial canal, crosses the medial side of the tympanic membrane, exits through the petrotympanic fissure and joins the lingual nerve. Cut in the middle ear, it removes taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue (and secretomotor drive to the submandibular and sublingual glands) while touch, carried by V3, is normal.
why: IX carries taste from the back third of the tongue.
The chorda tympani has already left VII by then, and the face would be weak.
It supplies the lower teeth, lip and chin.
It crosses the middle ear, carrying taste from the front of the tongue; general sensation stays with V3 in the lingual nerve.
An injury there would also take away touch and temperature.

likely.t: Tongue and palate nerves: V3 and chorda tympani in front, IX behind, X for the soft palate except the tensor veli palatini; palatal anesthesia

stem: Each of the following soft palate muscles is supplied by the vagus nerve EXCEPT the:
ex: All soft palate muscles are supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus except the tensor veli palatini (V3), which hooks around the pterygoid hamulus and also opens the auditory tube.
why: Supplied by X; it is the one tongue muscle not supplied by XII.
Supplied by V3 (nerve to the medial pterygoid); it is an arch 1 muscle.
Supplied by X through the pharyngeal plexus; it lifts the palate.
Supplied by X through the pharyngeal plexus.
Supplied by X through the pharyngeal plexus.

stem: A patient needs palatal anesthesia for scaling around the maxillary first and second molars. The injection is given near the greater palatine foramen. Which nerve is anesthetized?
ex: Palatal anesthesia: greater palatine nerve at the greater palatine foramen (medial to the second and third molars) for the palate from the molars to the canine; nasopalatine nerve at the incisive papilla for the palate behind the incisors.
why: It leaves the greater palatine foramen opposite the second and third molars and supplies the palatal mucosa and gingiva back to the canine.
It leaves the incisive foramen and supplies the palate behind the incisors.
It supplies the soft palate.
It supplies the molar teeth and their buccal gingiva, not the palatal mucosa.
It supplies the skin of the cheek and upper lip and, through its alveolar branches, the anterior teeth.

stem: True or false: The nasopalatine nerve reaches the palate through the greater palatine foramen to supply the mucosa behind the maxillary incisors.
ex: The nasopalatine nerve runs down the septum and through the incisive canal, emerging at the incisive foramen under the incisive papilla. The greater palatine foramen carries the greater palatine nerve.
why: The area behind the incisors is right, but the opening is the incisive foramen.
It emerges through the incisive foramen; the greater palatine foramen is for the greater palatine nerve.

stem:
A 50-year-old man has had painful swelling under the left side of his jaw for 3 weeks.
History: it gets worse at every meal and settles over an hour or two.
Findings: a firm, tender swelling below the left mandible; a hard lump can be felt in the floor of the mouth; little saliva comes from the left sublingual caruncle.
Which gland is involved, and why is it the most common site of this problem?
choices: Sublingual gland, because it has the most ducts
Minor salivary glands of the lip, because they are often injured
Submandibular gland, because its duct runs uphill and its saliva is thicker
Parotid gland, because its duct is the longest
Parotid gland, because it makes thick mucous saliva
ex: Most salivary stones form in the submandibular gland: its duct (Wharton) runs uphill to the sublingual caruncle and its saliva is thicker and more alkaline. Swelling at meals (mealtime syndrome) is typical.
why: Its many small ducts rarely form stones.
Injured lip glands form mucoceles, not mealtime swelling under the jaw.
