stem: In a randomized trial of a new mouthrinse, 1,000 patients are assigned to the rinse or a placebo. During the year, 100 stop using their rinse. The researchers analyze all 1,000 patients in the groups to which they were randomized. This is:
ex: Intention-to-treat keeps the groups as randomized and gives the most cautious, real-world estimate; per-protocol counts only completers and can overstate the benefit.
why: A per-protocol analysis would count only the 900 who used the rinse as planned.
Everyone is analyzed in the group they were randomized to, whether or not they finished, which keeps randomization's balance.
A subgroup analysis looks at one part of the sample, such as only the women.
An as-treated analysis would group people by what they actually used, not by their assignment.

stem: True or false: In a double-blind (double-masked) trial, neither the participants nor the clinicians assessing them know who received the treatment.
ex: Single-blind masks the participants; double-blind masks the participants and the clinicians or assessors. It keeps expectations from changing what patients report or how examiners score.
why: Masking both sides keeps expectations from changing how patients report or how examiners score.
That is the definition of double-blind; single-blind masks only the participants.

stem: During a periodontal study, one examiner records the same 4 mm pocket at a site every time she probes it. The calibrated examiners and the reference examiner all record 6 mm there. How would you describe her measurements?
ex: Precision is repeatability (reliability); accuracy is closeness to the truth (validity).
why: Her readings are far from the true value, and they are repeatable, the reverse of this.
She repeats herself, but the true depth is 6 mm.
She repeats her own reading every time (precision), but it is far from the true depth (accuracy).
Her readings agree with each other every time, which is precision.

likely.t: Standardization, calibration and reliability; precision versus accuracy

stem: To check a study's examiners, the same examiner charts a participant's pocket depths on Monday and again on Friday, and the two charts are compared. What is being measured?
ex: Intra-examiner: same examiner, different times. Inter-examiner: different examiners. Test-retest: the same questionnaire 1–2 weeks apart.
why: Inter-examiner reliability compares different examiners on the same patient.
Calibration is training examiners together on the same patients until their scores agree.
Test-retest reliability is for a questionnaire answered twice by the same person.
One examiner, the same patient, two times: intra-examiner reliability.

stem: A new caries-detection device is tested on 200 molars against histology. Of the 100 molars with caries, 90 test positive. Of the 100 sound molars, 20 test positive. What is the device's specificity?
why: That is the sensitivity: 90 of the 100 decayed molars detected.
That is the positive predictive value: 90 true positives of 110 positives.
Specificity is true negatives over everyone without disease: 80 of the 100 sound molars.
That is the negative predictive value: 80 true negatives of 90 negatives.
That is the false-positive rate (1 − specificity).

likely.t: Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values: calculating them and choosing a test for screening or confirming

stem: Which statement about diagnostic tests is false?
choices: A test's positive predictive value stays the same when the test is used where the disease is rarer
A negative result on a highly sensitive test helps rule the disease out
Specificity is the share of people without the disease whom the test correctly calls negative
Before an irreversible step such as an extraction, a highly specific test is preferred
ex: Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test; predictive values also depend on prevalence. Screen with sensitivity, confirm with specificity.
why: This is the false one: PPV falls as prevalence falls, because more of the positives are false. Sensitivity and specificity are the values that don't change.
This is true: high sensitivity means few false negatives (SnNout).
This is true: true negatives ÷ (true negatives + false positives).
This is true: few false positives means few healthy teeth treated (SpPin).

likely.t: Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values: calculating them and choosing a test for screening or confirming

stem: A cohort study reports that children who chew sugared gum daily have a relative risk of caries of 1.7 (95% CI 1.3–2.2) compared with children who don't. What does this mean?
choices: Daily gum chewers had a 1.7% higher risk of caries, and the result is not significant
Daily gum chewers had a 70% higher risk of caries, and the result is statistically significant
Daily gum chewing protected the children against caries, lowering their risk
The result is not significant, because the interval does not include 0
ex: RR = 1: no difference; above 1: harmful; below 1: protective. For a ratio, a 95% CI that excludes 1 is statistically significant.
why: A relative risk of 1.7 means 1.7 times the risk (70% higher), and an interval that excludes 1 is significant.
A relative risk of 1.7 is 1.7 times the risk, and an interval that excludes 1 is significant.
A relative risk above 1 is a harmful effect; below 1 would be protective.
For a ratio the null value is 1, not 0; this interval excludes 1, so it is significant.

likely.t: Reading relative risk, odds ratio, hazard ratio and NNT with their confidence intervals and p-values; type I and II errors and power

stem: True or false: A treatment with a hazard ratio of 0.92 (95% CI 0.83–1.02) significantly lowers the risk compared with control.
ex: The estimate suggests 8% lower risk, but the 95% interval runs from a 17% reduction to a 2% increase. Because it crosses 1, the data are consistent with no effect.
why: The point estimate suggests 8% lower risk, but the interval includes 1 (no difference), so the result is not significant.
Because the 95% CI crosses 1, the data are consistent with no effect: not statistically significant.

likely.t: Reading relative risk, odds ratio, hazard ratio and NNT with their confidence intervals and p-values; type I and II errors and power

stem: In a two-year trial, 25% of the children in the control group and 15% of the children in a sealant program develop new caries. How many children must be in the program to prevent one child from developing caries?
ex: NNT = 1/ARR. Note how a 40% relative reduction is a 10-point absolute one.
why: That is 1 ÷ 0.25, the control group's risk alone, not the difference.
40% is the relative risk reduction (0.10 ÷ 0.25), not the NNT.
That is about 1 ÷ 0.15, the treated group's risk alone.

stem: Of 400 adults with diabetes in a practice, 100 have periodontitis. What are the risk and the odds of periodontitis in this group?
ex: Risk = events ÷ everyone in the group. Odds = events ÷ non-events.
why: Risk = 100 ÷ 400 = 0.25; odds = 100 with it ÷ 300 without it = 0.33.
These are swapped: risk divides by everyone (400), odds by those without the disease (300).
Odds divide by the 300 without the disease, not by all 400.
These describe not having periodontitis (300 of 400; 300 to 100).

stem:
Which statements about significance and error are true?
1. A larger sample size raises a study's power.
2. A type I error is failing to detect a difference that really exists.
3. Alpha, usually set at 0.05, is the accepted chance of a type I error.
4. A statistically significant result is always clinically important.
ex: Type I (alpha): a false positive. Type II (beta): a false negative. Power, one minus beta, rises with a bigger sample. Significance is not importance.
why: Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false: that is a type II error; a type I error is finding a difference that isn't real. Statement 4 is false: a tiny difference can be significant in a large trial yet too small to matter to patients.
It includes 4, which is false: a tiny difference can be significant in a large trial yet too small to matter to patients.

It includes 2, which is false: that is a type II error; a type I error is finding a difference that isn't real. It leaves out 1, which is true: more participants make a real difference easier to detect.

stem: True or false: Two sets of data with the same mean can have very different standard deviations.
ex: The mean is the center; the standard deviation is the spread around it. A tall, narrow curve and a low, wide one can share a mean.
why: The mean shows the center and the standard deviation the spread, which can differ widely around the same center.
The statement is right: the same center doesn't mean the same spread.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The odds ratio is the measure of association usually reported by a prospective cohort study.
2. When an outcome is rare, the odds ratio approximates the relative risk.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Cohort studies and trials follow people forward and report relative risk; case-control studies can't compute incidence and report odds ratios. With few events, odds and risk are nearly equal, so the two ratios converge.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: a cohort follows exposed and unexposed people forward and reports relative risk; the odds ratio is the case-control study's measure.
Statement 2 is true, not false: with few events, odds and risk are nearly equal, so the two ratios converge.

stem: Each of the following increases a study's power EXCEPT:
choices: Enrolling more participants in each group
Studying a larger true difference between the groups
Reducing variability with calibrated, accurate measurements
ex: Power = 1 − beta. It rises with sample size, effect size, lower variability, better measurement and a looser alpha.
why: A larger sample raises power.
A bigger effect is easier to detect.
A stricter alpha makes significance harder to reach, so power falls.
Less noise in the data raises power.

stem:
Study: randomized trial of 20,000 adults
Comparison: a new toothpaste versus a standard toothpaste for six months
Result: the gingival index fell 0.02 points more with the new toothpaste (p < 0.001)
Scale: the index runs from 0 to 3
What is the best reading of this result?
choices: Not statistically significant, because the difference between the toothpastes is so small
Statistically significant, but probably too small to matter clinically
Clinically important, because a p-value this small shows a large benefit for patients
Proof that the new toothpaste will improve the gums of every patient who uses it
ex: Statistical significance is not clinical significance: judge the size of the effect and its confidence interval, and whether it matters to patients.
why: The p-value is far below 0.05, so it is significant; small and significant can go together in a huge trial.
A huge trial can make a trivial difference significant; 0.02 on a 0-to-3 scale is unlikely to matter to patients.
A p-value says nothing about how big an effect is.
A trial estimates an average effect; it doesn't promise a result for each patient.
